newsitem.title: CANADA: Delgratia involved in latest mining scam.
newsitem.headline: Delgratia involved in latest mining scam.

text.p: Delgratia Mining Corp. Monday revealed the latest mining scandal involving a Canadian company, reporting insignificant amounts of gold and evidence of sample tampering at its Nevada property.

Delgratia, whose Josh Deposit in southern Nevada has been awash in controversy since March, said an audit by independent consultants showed it was a victim of fraud known as salting, in which gold from other sources is added to mine samples.

"We conclude that there is insignificant gold contained in the Josh Deposit and that any gold detected beyond background amounts was introduced into the samples after they had been collected at the drill," said a report by consulting engineers Brian Mountford and Morris Beattie.

The deposit had once been touted by a company official as harboring as much as 5 million ounces of gold, an estimate questioned in March when Nevada state mining officials said not enough drilling had been done to back up the claim.
Stock in Delgratia, a company associated with controversial one-time Arakis Energy Corp. Chief Executive Terry Alexander, was halted on Nasdaq. It closed on Friday at $12.

Delgratia owns 40 percent of in the Josh project, with the rest owned by British Virgin Islands firm Philgold Investments Inc., which is indirectly owned by Delgratia Chairman Charles Ager and his family.
The news came hard on the heels of two other salting scandals involving Canadian mining firms.
The most famous was Bre-X Minerals Ltd.'s stunning revelation early this month that its Busang property in Indonesia -- once touted as the world's largest gold deposit -- was worthless.
Calgary-based Bre-X, whose shares had soared to C$28 ($20.44) after a 10-for-one split and are now worth pennies, said it was the victim of a massive fraud by unidentified parties.
Last week Golden Rule Resources Ltd., also of Calgary, lost half its market value when tests on its venture project in Ghana suggested results from earlier tests were overstated.
Delgratia, based in Vancouver, British Columbia, said its consultants identified the likely source of the tampering and that it did not involve anyone from the company.

"It is now clear that the company has been the victim of data falsification," Ager said in a statement. He said his company was asking U.S. law enforcement officials to investigate the possibility of criminal activity.
Ager was not available for comment but his son, company spokesman Carl Ager, said Delgratia had not suspected any of the results prior to their release.
"Basically, it was a shock," Carl Ager said. "We've been victimized somehow."
Several analysts and fund managers expressed doubts about Delgratia and its deposit in March when company claims of a major find were disputed by mining officials in Nevada.

The company's stock plunged to $16 from $33.63 before being halted on March 21 and Ager was forced to say it was premature to make estimates of the deposit's size. At the time, however, he expressed confidence in the project.
Alexander was president of Delgratia until last year and is now acting as a consultant for the company, Carl Ager said.

Alexander made headlines in 1995 when he excited investors with plans for a pipeline -- financed by a Saudi prince -- that would make a major Sudan oil field a producing reality. Eventually, the financing deal, and Arakis' stock price, went bust and Alexander left the company.
Delgratia said Charles Ager planned personally to fund a review of all data associated with the Josh fiasco.
